13-315.r: E-mail attachment → any digital file: documents, text files, music, audio, video, photos (all of the above).

13-318.r: Blog = Web + log → a publicly accessible personal journal web page; its writer is a blogger.

13-319.r: Executing → the process of carrying out commands; CPU work in four parts: Fetch → Decode → Execute → Write back (store).
13-319.h: F-D-E-W: Fetch, Decode, Execute, Write back.

13-320.r: A 'menu' → contains a list of related commands.

13-321.r: Bookmark → saves a favourite website in your browser for quick access later.

13-322.r: Size of virtual memory → depends on disc space (space allocated on hard disk); it speeds exchange between hard disk and RAM.

13-323.r: ICT = Information and Communications Technology → internet, wireless networks, cellphones and other communication media.

13-324.r: SIM = Subscriber Identity Module → small card holding the subscriber's account information; used in GSM and UMTS handsets.

13-325.r: SMS = Short Messaging Service → exchanging messages by mobile phone.

13-326.r: A picture message stays in a mobile's private inbox for up to 30 days; save it to the message box to keep it longer.

13-327.r: Wrong pair: Android – Voice input; Android is Google's touch-screen mobile OS (Linux kernel). Correct: Optic fibres – light waves; LHC – God particle; Red Planet – Mars.

13-329.r: Apple iPhone 4S → 8 hours talk time on 3G and voice assistant Siri; standby was 200 hours (not 300) and RAM 512 MB (not 640).

13-330.r: Cyber venting → using websites to pour out one's grievances (e.g. about one's employer), often anonymously.

13-331.r: Denial of Service (DOS) attack → floods a website or server with fake traffic so legitimate users cannot access it.

13-333.r: DDoS (Distributed Denial-of-Service) → a cyber attack that floods a target server or network with Internet traffic from many different sources.

13-334.r: Hacking → exploiting vulnerabilities to gain unauthorized access to a system or resources; neither searching nor security (none of these).

13-335.r: Computer hacker (security hacker) → violates computer security with malicious intent for personal gain, using bugs or exploits.

13-336.r: Cracker → breaks into computer systems without authorization and deliberately defaces websites for a fraudulent purpose.

13-337.r: Crackers → also called black hat hackers; break computer security without authority to damage systems, commit fraud, steal identity.

13-338.r: Cracker (black hat hacker) → gains unauthorized access, destroys vital data, denies legitimate users' service for personal gain.
13-338.t: Don't confuse crackers with white hat hackers, who are security specialists employed to use hacking.

13-339.r: Virtual keyboard (software, no physical keys) → reduces keystroke logging; protects against password theft, Trojan programs and spyware (all of the above).

13-340.r: Cybercrime → includes hacking, cyberstalking and denial of service attacks (all of the above).

13-341.r: Online chatting → not a cybercrime; phishing, cyber stalking and identity theft are cybercrimes.

13-342.r: Phishing → deceptive emails or text messages that trick users into revealing sensitive information (passwords, account numbers) or installing malicious software.

13-344.r: Spoofing → an e-mail that appears to come from one source but is sent from another; criminal disguises email address, phone number or URL.

13-345.r: Two essential features of cybercrime → offender's computer skills and victim's ignorance of computer technology.

13-346.r: Cyber security features → compliance, defence against internal threats, threat prevention (all of the above); also external-threat coverage, cloud security, analytics.

13-347.r: First cyber law for e-commerce in India → Information Technology Act, 2000 (enacted 9 June, in force 17 October 2000); recognises e-records and digital signatures.

13-348.r: Reporting cybersecurity incidents to CERT-In is mandatory for service providers, data centres and body corporate (Section 70-B, IT Act 2000; IT Rules 2013).

13-349.r: Individual cyber insurance covers → restoring a malware-hit computer, consultant for cyber extortion, court defence in third-party suits; not a new computer after wilful damage.

13-350.r: GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) → adopted by the European Union in April 2016, implemented from 25 May 2018; replaced the 1995 Data Protection Directive.

13-351.r: Confidentiality → data security principle protecting customer and organisation data from unauthorized access or use; others: integrity, availability, accountability, non-repudiation.

13-352.r: BIOS (Basic Input-Output System) → resides in the ROM.

13-353.r: Networking of computers → increases utility and information access, but also security threats like hacking and viruses (all of the above).

13-354.r: Resilience → ability of a computer network to recover from errors like connection failure or data loss and keep offering services.

13-355.r: Data systems for planning → Decision Support System (DSS), an information system that supports decision making.

13-356.r: Speedometer of a car → an analog computer.

13-357.r: Software → written programs (machine-readable instructions) that make a computer work in the desired way.

13-358.r: Another name for computer programs → computer software; two major types: application software and system software.

13-359.r: 'Basic Unit' → not a computer component; main parts: input/output devices, processing unit, memory unit, secondary storage.

13-360.r: Microsoft → a software developing organization; founded by Bill Gates and Paul Allen on 4 April 1975; headquarters in Washington.

13-361.r: Wipro → founder chairman Azim Premji ('Czar of Indian IT'); his son Rishad Premji became executive chairman in July 2019.

13-362.r: CEOs (question period): Google → Sundar Pichai; Microsoft → Satya Nadella; Twitter → Parag Agarwal (till October 2022); Adobe → Shantanu Narayen.

13-363.r: Twitter → created by Jack Dorsey (with Noah Glass, Biz Stone, Evan Williams) in March 2006; Dorsey was CEO 2015–2021; later rebranded as X.

13-364.r: Facebook → co-founded by Mark Zuckerberg; parent company Meta Platforms owns Facebook, Instagram, Threads and WhatsApp.

13-365.r: LinkedIn → social networking site for professionals and business people (employees and employers).

13-366.r: E-commerce advantages → ability to operate 24/7, extensive reach, personalised shopping, lower operational costs.

13-367.r: India's biggest E-commerce company (per the book) → M-Junction, a 50:50 joint venture of SAIL and Tata Steel; world's largest online steel marketplace; Kolkata-based.

13-368.r: Flipkart, Alibaba, Amazon → primarily B2C (sell directly to consumers); the book accepts both B2C and B2B, as they also serve third-party sellers.
